newsitem.title: USA: Texans set to fill final three U.S. House seats.
newsitem.headline: Texans set to fill final three U.S. House seats.

text.p: Texas voters return to the polls Tuesday in congressional districts holding run-off elections to fill the final three seats in the newly elected U.S. House of Representatives.

In the run-off elections, called after no candidates won majorities in November voting, Republicans were assured of picking up at least one House seat as two Republican candidates square off in Texas' 8th district.

But incumbents from both parties were battling for a return ticket to Washington from two other southeast Texas districts, where voters have been treated to campaigns spiced with claims of voter fraud.

Texas pollsters expected voting to be light in the three districts, among 13 redrawn in Texas by a federal court panel following a ruling that the boundary lines of three neighboring districts had been racially manipulated.
"(Turnout) is certainly not going to be at general election levels," said Harris County Clerk Beverly Kaufman. "I'm projecting a total of about 10 percent," she said.

In the 9th district, where Rep. Steve Stockman is battling for a second term in Congress, federal poll watchers were expected to monitor voting because of complaints black voters were being harassed and likely Republican voters were enticed to the polls with offers of a chance to win free turkeys and hams.

Supporters of Democratic challenger Nick Lampson alleged poll watchers working for the Stockman campaign were harassing blacks during early voting that ended Friday, and asked U.S. Attorney General Janet Reno to send federal monitors into the district.

A Stockman aide said the Republican poll watchers were put in place to stem voter fraud by the district's "Democratic machine." "There is a huge amount of voter fraud by Democrats in our district," campaign aide Cory Birenbaum said.
Dubbed "Congressman Clueless" by a Texas magazine, Stockman told supporters he was trailing.
"If the election were over today we would lose," he said in an 11th-hour appeal for support in the district stretching from east Houston to the Louisiana border.

Lampson, a Beaumont Democrat with strong union support in this largely blue-collar district dotted with refineries and chemical plants, spent the run-off campaign blasting Stockman over his ties to militia groups and support for cuts in Medicare spending.

In the neighboring district, incumbent Democrat Rep. Ken Bentsen, nephew of former senator and Treasury Secretary Lloyd Bentsen, spent the final week of a run-off campaign defending his record on Medicare and Social Security spending.

Bentsen's challenger in the Houston-area district, Republican Dolly Madison McKenna, also dusted off an old Republican campaign tactic, alleging the Bentsen campaign was funded by "organized crime" for accepting contributions from a union political action committee.

The Laborers' International Union of North America, which contributed $11,000 to the Bentsen campaign, has been monitored by the Justice Department since February 1995 for admitted ties between union officers and suspected mobsters.
"She has gone off the deep end on this one," Bentsen said.

In the 8th district north of Houston, Spring physician Gene Fontenot spent more than $1 million of his own money against Kevin Brady. The two Republicans are battling for a seat vacated by Rep. Jack Fields.
Brady, a state Representative from The Woodlands, pulled down 41 percent to Fontenot's 39 percent in November voting in the district stretching from Houston's northern suburbs to College Station.

The races will not tip the balance of power in Congress, where the Republicans held a 227-205 majority in the House following the November general elections. That figure includes a seat reserved on the Republican side of the aisle for the winner from Texas' 8th district.

The run-off elections were called by a federal panel that redrew 13 Texas districts after the spring primaries. The panel opened the November ballot to all comers and ordered the Dec. 10 elections in districts where no candidate captured a majority.
